extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional historians, and educated general readers interested in comparative constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective political-essay analyzing the comparative structure and practical effects of constitutional arrangements (especially executive powers) in the British and American systems, with focus on dissolution, creation of peers, and divided sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singleness and unity of sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: How important singleness and unity are in political action; the English Constitution is the type of SIMPLE Constitutions, in which the ultimate power upon all questions is in the hands of the same persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity enables coherent policy and decisive action across legislative and administrative questions; a single sovereign authority facilitates implementing the will of the people because it appoints and can remove the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of sovereign authority leads to indecision
rubrics_metrics.description: The splitting of sovereignty into many parts amounts to there being no sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sovereign authority is divided (as in the American Constitution), critical decisions can be blocked by competing bodies; example: inability to settle post-war reconstruction because President and Congress could each block the other's course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety-valve: executive power to create peers (augment the revising chamber)
rubrics_metrics.description: The head of the executive can overcome the resistance of the second chamber by choosing new members of that chamber; if he do not find a majority, he can make a majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts as a constitutional 'safety-valve' allowing the popular will carried by the executive to be effectuated despite upper-chamber resistance. It is useful but dangerous: it 'lets forth a dangerous accumulation of inhibited power', and can be used incrementally (habitual creations) or reserved as a decisive magic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulator: power of dissolving the popular chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of dissolving the otherwise sovereign chamber confided to the chief executive serves as a regulator of Parliamentary caprice, party violence, and selfishness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissolution allows appeal from one Parliament to another (Parliament No.1 to Parliament No.2) and thus checks caprice and factionalism. Its effective exercise depends on who wields it and the political context; practice has concentrated its use in the Premier rather than the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary vice — caprice
rubrics_metrics.description: Caprice is the commonest and most formidable vice of a choosing chamber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capricious assemblies shift governments frequently, producing instability. The remedy of dissolution is meant to check caprice, but its efficacy depends on the institutional design of who may dissolve and when.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary vice — party organisation causing sectarian government
rubrics_metrics.description: The only mode by which a cohesive majority and a lasting administration can be upheld is party organisation; but that organisation itself tends to aggravate party violence and party animosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party cohesion gives stable government but risks sectarian rule and heightened partisanship; this tradeoff must be managed by constitutional mechanisms (checks, appeals to electorate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary vice — selfishness and special interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A Parliament, like every other sort of sovereign, has peculiar feelings, peculiar prejudices, peculiar interests; and it may pursue these in opposition to the desires, and even in opposition to the well-being of the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-interest and jobbery in assemblies can harm national interest; external or institutional checks are needed to curb such tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who best checks caprice: the Premier (internal appointee)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Premier himself is the person most interested in maintaining his administration, and therefore the most likely person to use efficiently and dexterously the power by which it is to be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Premier bears the cost of losing office, he is well-placed to use dissolution carefully to check Parliamentary caprice. An extrinsic monarch may encourage intrigues and be unreliable in checking Parliament's caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who best checks party zeal and selfishness: an extrinsic impartial authority (king/colonial governor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The party zeal and the self-seeking of Parliament are best checked by an authority which has no connection with Parliament or dependence upon it—supposing that such authority is morally and intellectually equal to the performance of the entrusted function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An impartial external authority (e.g., a constitutional monarch or colonial governor) can restrain party excesses. But such authorities often lack local attachment and permanent interest, and may govern for their own career-preserving reasons, producing other defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required in a head exercising dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: To know that Parliament is wrong, a man must be, if not a great statesman, yet a considerable statesman... He must have great natural vigour... He must have incessant industry...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective use of dissolution requires a capable, industrious, and politically discerning person; ordinary hereditary monarchs are often ill-fit (badly educated for business, spoiled by palace life), so the power's beneficial exercise is unlikely in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes and limits of executive power within mixed constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Constitution subdivides authority (states' sovereignty, Congress vs. President, Senate treaty power), producing multiple repositories (e.g., President can veto, Congress can override; Senate controls treaties; President may exercise 'war power' such as issuing paper money).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdivision can prevent tyranny but may impede decisive action in crises. Legal precedents (e.g., presidential emission of paper money as part of 'war power') show how practical exigencies can expand executive reach, sometimes contrary to formal allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of constitutional checks depends on national political maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: The dangers arising from a party spirit in Parliament exceeding that of the nation, and of a selfishness in Parliament contradicting the true interest of the nation, are not great dangers in a country where the mind of the nation is steadily political, and where its control over its representatives is constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In politically mature, attentive societies, public opinion and vigilance limit Parliamentary excesses; in early or scattered communities (great distances, weak public attention) institutional checks (dissolution, external authority) are more essential.
